He came to my office with lists of objections, printed out, numbered. We worked through them one at a time, and I answered them as honestly as I could, and every answer that satisfied him produced two more objections by the following week. I began to understand that we were not actually engaged in an argument. We were engaged in a ritual, and the ritual let him keep his distance from the thing he was circling.

One afternoon I put down the list. I asked him about his marriage, which I knew was failing, and about his father, who had died the year before without the two of them ever reconciling. He got very quiet, and then he told me things that had nothing to do with the cosmological argument, about a grief he could not put down and a guilt he could not resolve and a fear that if there was a God, that God had every reason to reject him. And I understood, finally, what the two years of arguments had been about. He was not afraid the faith was false. He was afraid it was true, and that if it was true, he would have to face a God he assumed would condemn him. The objections were armor against the acceptance he did not believe he could receive.

We never finished the list. What happened instead was that he heard, slowly, that the God he was arguing against was not the God who was actually there, that the gospel is precisely the announcement that the God who has every right to reject you has instead come to find you, that the father who died unreconciled is not the pattern of the Father who runs down the road to meet the son who wrecked everything. The arguments did not reach him. The gospel did, once we stopped pretending the arguments were the point. He believes now. Not because I won the debate. Because he finally let himself be found by the thing he had been arguing against, which turned out to be love rather than the judgment he had armored himself against.

## What Actually Reaches the Doubter

If arguments are not enough, what is. Three things, in my experience, reach places the arguments cannot. The first is presence, the steady, unhurried presence of people who believe and who do not flinch at your doubt. Faith is caught more than it is taught, and the doubter who is loved by believers over years absorbs something the debates never delivered. The early church did not grow because it out-argued the Roman philosophers. It grew because, as the pagan critics themselves complained, these Christians loved in a way that could not be explained, caring for plague victims that everyone else abandoned. The love was the argument the arguments could not make.

The second is honesty about suffering. The doubter is often waiting to see whether the faith can survive contact with real pain, and a triumphant apologetics that has no room for the dark answers the wrong question. What reaches them is a believer who has suffered and still believes, not because they resolved the problem of evil but because they met God inside the suffering rather than on the far side of it. Bonhoeffer writing from a Nazi prison, still believing, reaches a doubter in a way that a clever argument never will, because Bonhoeffer's faith was tested in the exact fire the doubter fears.

The third is prayer, the actual practice of addressing God even in unbelief, the way the father in Mark 9 addressed Jesus while still confessing his unbelief. I tell doubters to pray the honest prayer, the prayer that says I am not sure you are there, but if you are, I am asking you to make yourself known. That is not intellectual dishonesty. It is the exact opposite. It is running the one experiment that the detached analysis refuses to run, which is to address the person and see whether he answers. I have watched that prayer answered more times than I can count. Not with an argument. With a presence the argument could never have produced.

## When the Doubt Has Teeth

For some, the failure of the arguments is not an intellectual curiosity but a source of real anguish, a sense that they have tried everything and God has still not come, and the not-coming feels like rejection by a God they cannot even be sure exists. If that is you, hear this. The silence you are experiencing is not proof of God's absence, and it is not proof of your failure. The whole tradition is full of people who cried into a silence and were not abandoned, only waiting in a dark they could not yet see through.

And if the anguish has grown into something heavier, if the failure of your search has left you feeling that there is no point in continuing at all, please stop the search tonight and reach for a person instead of an argument. A crisis line, a friend, a counselor, a pastor. The despair is not a conclusion your reasoning reached. It is an exhaustion your soul is suffering, and it lies about how permanent the dark is. You do not owe anyone a resolved doubt. You owe yourself the phone call that keeps you here until the light, which always comes, comes back.

## The Verdict

The arguments are good and they are not enough, and discovering that they are not enough is not a failure of your faith or your intellect. It is a discovery of what faith actually is, which is trust in a person rather than the conclusion of a proof. You can win every debate and remain unmoved, because the doubt was never really living in the debate. It was living in a wound, a fear, a hunger the arguments could not reach.

So put down the next book for a while. You have enough arguments. What you need now is the thing the arguments were always pointing toward and never were, which is the actual encounter. Pray the honest prayer. Let yourself be loved by people who believe. Watch for God in the suffering rather than demanding he prove himself before it. The man who found me was not an argument, though the arguments cleared my path to him. He was a Father, and he reached the exact place no argument could, because that place was never going to be reached by anything less than him.

chapters.title: When Scripture Reads You
chapters.summary: You sit down to read the Bible. If you stay long enough, the direction reverses, and the text begins to read you.
chapters.body:
> "For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and of spirit, of joints and of marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart." (Hebrews 4:12)

You approach the Bible as the reader. You are the subject, the text is the object, you hold it and study it and extract from it what you came for. That is the natural posture, and it is the one we bring to every other book. We are the ones doing the reading. The book sits still and lets itself be read. We are in control of the encounter.

But something strange happens if you stay with Scripture long enough. The direction reverses. You come to a passage intending to read it, and midway through you realize it is reading you. The verse you meant to analyze has turned and is analyzing you. The word you came to master has quietly become the word that is exposing you, and you are no longer the subject of the sentence. You are the object.

Hebrews names this exactly. The word of God is living and active. Living. It is not inert text waiting for you to act on it. It acts. It is sharper than a two-edged sword, and it pierces, and it divides, and it discerns the thoughts and intentions of the heart. Discerns. The word does the discerning. You thought you were examining it, and the whole time it was examining you.

I have felt this and been unsettled by it. I have sat down to prepare a sermon, to handle the text professionally, to work on it, and been stopped cold by a verse that turned and worked on me instead, that named a thing in my own heart I had been keeping in the dark, that I had no intention of surrendering when I opened the book. I came to use the text. The text used me. That is not a failure of Bible study. That is Bible study succeeding.

Because this is finally the difference between reading Scripture and being formed by it. As long as you remain the reader, in control, extracting, you can keep the text at arm's length and manage what it is allowed to touch. But when you let it become living and active, when you stop protecting yourself from it, it moves past your defenses to the marrow, to the intentions you did not plan to expose, and it begins to change you rather than merely inform you.

So do not always come to Scripture as the one in charge. Come sometimes with the posture reversed. Come not to master the text but to be examined by it, not to extract but to be exposed, and stay long enough for the direction to flip. The word is living. It will read you if you let it.

You opened the book to read it. Stay, and let it read you.

chapters.title: When Your Entire Community Believes and You Don't
chapters.summary: You are surrounded by people who are sure, and you are the only one in the room who isn't. The isolation of hidden doubt is its own kind of suffering. Here is how to survive the room without lying in it.
chapters.body:
There is a specific loneliness that has no name in most churches. It is the loneliness of the person who sits in the pew every week surrounded by people who seem entirely sure, singing songs about a certainty they no longer feel, shaking hands after the service and saying they are fine, and going home to a house where the doubt waits for them like an animal. The community believes. They do not. And they have learned that saying so out loud would cost them everyone they love.

I have sat with these people, and what strikes me every time is how alone they are in the middle of a crowd. It is one thing to doubt in a secular city where no one cares. It is another thing entirely to doubt inside a family, a small town, a church that is your entire social world, where your unbelief is not just your private problem but a threat to every relationship you have. That person is not weak. That person is carrying a weight most of the confident people around them have never had to lift.

## The Sociology of Sacred Certainty

The sociologist Peter Berger described in his 1967 work The Sacred Canopy how communities construct what he called plausibility structures, the social scaffolding that makes a belief feel obvious and unquestionable. A belief held by everyone around you feels like a fact. A belief held by no one around you feels like madness, even if it is true. The point Berger made, which cuts both ways, is that certainty is often a social product rather than an intellectual one. The people in your church who seem so sure are, in part, sure because everyone around them is sure. Their certainty is being held up by the same social pressure that is crushing you.

This matters because it means your doubt is not necessarily a sign that you see less than they do. It may be a sign that you see more. You have stepped outside the plausibility structure enough to notice that it is a structure, and the vertigo you feel is the vertigo of standing where the ground is not being held up for you by the crowd. That is a terrifying place to stand. It is also, sometimes, the place where the most honest faith is finally forged, because a faith that survives outside the crowd's support is a faith you actually own rather than one you inherited.

I say this carefully, because I do not want to flatter your doubt into a badge of superiority. That is its own trap. The person who thinks their unbelief makes them smarter than the believers around them has simply traded one social pride for another. But I do want to break the equation that doubt equals defect. Sometimes the one person in the room who is not sure is the one person in the room who is taking God seriously enough to be honest about the difficulty.

## The Faith the Crowd Never Tested

Consider what it means that the confident people around you have often never been tested the way you are being tested. A faith held up by a crowd has never had to stand on its own legs. It has never known whether it could survive the withdrawal of social approval, because the approval has never been withdrawn. This is not a criticism of those believers. It is simply an observation about the difference between a belief that has been load-tested and a belief that has not. Yours is being load-tested right now, in the worst possible conditions, and the fact that it hurts is not evidence that it is failing. It is evidence that it is being examined more rigorously than the comfortable faith around you has ever been.

The theologian Miroslav Volf, writing in his 1996 book Exclusion and Embrace out of the wreckage of the war in his native Croatia, observed that faith which has never been threatened has never had to become its own, that it remains borrowed until the moment it is contested. Volf was writing about faith under the pressure of ethnic hatred and violence, but the principle reaches your quieter situation. Until your faith is contested, it belongs to the crowd that gave it to you. When it is contested, and you either lose it or make it your own, it becomes for the first time genuinely yours. The doubter in the confident room is standing at the exact threshold where inherited faith either dies or becomes personal, and that threshold is a more honest place to stand than the comfortable middle of the crowd.

I do not say this to romanticize your pain. I say it to reframe what it means. You have assumed that your doubt places you below the confident believers, at the bottom of the spiritual hierarchy of the room. It may place you somewhere else entirely, at the one point in the room where faith is actually being decided rather than merely inherited. That is a lonely place. It is not a lesser place. Some of the deepest believers I have ever known passed through exactly this valley, and they came out with a faith that could no longer be taken from them, precisely because it had already survived being alone.

## The Cost of the Mask

The mask is exhausting. You know this if you wear it. Every conversation is a small performance. Every prayer meeting is a rehearsal of words you no longer mean. Every time someone asks how your walk with God is going, you produce a sentence that keeps the peace and deepens the loneliness. And the deepest cruelty is this. The very community that could hold you, that exists in theory precisely to carry the ones who are struggling, is the community you cannot tell, because you have learned that struggling is not permitted here.

> "Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ." (Galatians 6:2)

Read that verse and then look at your church and ask an honest question. Is this a community that bears burdens, or a community that hides them. Because a church where you cannot admit doubt is not bearing your burden. It is requiring you to hide it, which is the opposite of what Paul commands. That is not a failure on your part. It is a failure of the church's culture, and naming it as such is not bitterness. It is accuracy. A community that only accepts the certain has excluded most of the people the gospel was written for.

## Why I Understand the Mask From Both Sides

I came to faith from atheism, which means for most of my life I was the unbeliever surrounded by believers who thought I was one of them or wished I would become one. I know the resentment of being handed certainties by people who had never doubted. And I was raised without a father, so I know the particular hunger of a person who wants to belong somewhere and fears that honesty will cost them the belonging. Those two experiences taught me not to trust a community that only has room for the confident, because I was never confident, and the communities that had no room for me were the ones I was right to keep my distance from.

But here is the turn. When Christ finally found me, he did not find me in a room full of certain people. He found me in my honesty, in the middle of my objections, in the place where I had stopped performing anything for anyone. The God of the Bible is not afraid of the doubter. He is afraid, if I can put it that way, of the liar, the one who has so mastered the performance of faith that they have deceived even themselves. Jesus was gentle with doubt and hard on hypocrisy. That should tell the doubter in the confident room exactly where they stand with God, whatever they stand with the crowd.

## Finding the One Safe Person

You do not need to tell the whole community. That is a common mistake, to think the only alternative to hiding from everyone is confessing to everyone. You do not owe your doubt to the crowd. What you need, and what will actually begin to break the isolation, is one safe person. One. A single human being who can hear the true sentence and not flinch, not fix, not report you to the elders, not treat you as a project. One person changes everything, because the doubt that is spoken to one trusted human loses its power to define you in secret.

Finding that person takes discernment, and sometimes they are not inside your immediate community. Sometimes the safe person is a pastor from another church, a counselor, a friend who left the faith and can hold your doubt without either celebrating it or panicking at it. The theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer, writing his 1938 book Life Together about a community that would soon be scattered by the Gestapo, argued that the Christian who cannot be alone should beware of community, and the Christian who cannot be in community should beware of being alone. You need both. You need the solitude to be honest with God without an audience, and you need the one person who proves that honesty does not equal exile.

## When Leaving Feels Like the Only Air

Some who read this have concluded that the only way to be honest is to leave, to walk away from the community entirely, because staying means lying and lying is unbearable. I understand the logic, and I will not tell you it is always wrong. Sometimes a community is so hostile to honesty that staying really would require the death of your integrity, and no faith is worth that price. But I will offer one caution, learned from watching many people walk this road.

The people who leave in a burst of relief often discover, a year later, that they traded one loneliness for another. They escaped the loneliness of hiding among believers and inherited the loneliness of having no one who shares the deepest questions of their life. The doubt did not resolve by leaving. It just lost the last people who might have walked with it. So before you leave, ask whether the problem is the faith or the community's handling of it, because those are different problems, and leaving solves at most one of them. Sometimes the answer is a different church, not no church. Sometimes it is finding the honest remnant inside the church you have. Leaving should be a considered decision, not an escape from a room you were never given permission to be honest in.

I say this as a man who spent years outside every believing community and knows exactly what that costs. Being raised without a father, I learned early to be the person on the edge of every room, watching, never fully belonging, and I carried that into my years as an atheist, where I told myself the distance was freedom. It was not freedom. It was exile with a better name. When people describe the relief of walking away from a church that suffocated their honesty, I believe them, and I also know what waits on the other side, because I lived there, and the loneliness of the empty room is not less than the loneliness of the crowded one. It is only quieter, and quiet loneliness is easier to mistake for peace.

So I do not tell people never to leave. I tell them to count the cost honestly, both costs, the cost of staying dishonest and the cost of leaving lonely, and to make sure that whatever they choose, they do not do it alone and do not do it in a single wounded night. The decision to leave a community is one of the most significant a person makes, and it deserves to be made in daylight, with counsel, over time, and not as a reflex against a room that hurt. Wounds heal badly when the treatment is only escape.

## The Weight I Will Not Lift Off You

If your doubt has curdled into something heavier, if the isolation has convinced you that you are fundamentally alone in the universe and that the aloneness is unbearable, please hear this before you read another word. That feeling is real and it is also lying to you about its permanence. You are not the only one, even if you are the only one in your particular pew. And the weight you are carrying is not a weight you were built to carry by yourself. If the darkness has started to whisper that everyone would be better off without you, that is the exhaustion talking, not the truth, and it is time to tell someone tonight. A crisis line, a doctor, a friend, anyone with a pulse who will stay on the phone. You do not have to solve the theology first. You just have to not be alone with the dark right now.

The despair is a liar with a very specific lie, which is that no one could understand and no one would stay. I have watched that lie proven false a hundred times. The moment the true sentence leaves your mouth to a safe person, the lie loses its footing, because it turns out someone can hear it and stay. Give someone that chance. Deny the isolation the silence it feeds on.

## The Verdict

Being the only doubter in a room full of the certain is one of the loneliest positions in the Christian life, and the loneliness is not a punishment for your unbelief. It is a symptom of a community that has made no room for the very struggle the gospel was built to hold. You are not less faithful than the confident crowd. You may simply be more honest, and honesty in a dishonest room always feels like isolation.

Find the one safe person. Keep the solitude that lets you be honest with God without an audience. And do not mistake the community's failure to hold your doubt for God's refusal to hold it. The God who found me outside every certain room is not waiting for you inside the crowd's certainty. He is waiting in your honesty, which is the one place the crowd never taught you he could be. Go there. He is already there, and he is not alone in the way you have been.

chapters.title: When Your Family Thinks You've Lost Your Mind
chapters.summary: Faith transitions do not happen in isolation. They happen in families. And the family that cannot hold theological difference cannot hold each other.
chapters.body:
The phone call comes on a Sunday afternoon. Your mother's voice is tight with a concern she is trying to disguise as casual conversation. She heard from your sister that you have stopped attending the church you were raised in. Or she noticed that you did not bow your head at Thanksgiving dinner. Or your father found a book on your shelf, Ehrman, or Enns, or Zahnd, that signals a departure from the theological world they inhabit. The conversation that follows is one of the most painful in the human repertoire, because it is a conversation in which the people who love you most become convinced that you are in danger, and the danger they perceive is your own thinking.

Faith transitions, the shifts in belief, practice, affiliation, or theological framework that happen throughout the course of a human life, are among the most common and least discussed sources of family conflict in American culture. The reason they are so volatile is that they touch something deeper than opinion. For the family that has organized its identity around a shared faith, a member's departure from that faith is not merely a change of mind. It is experienced as a betrayal, a death, a rejection of the family itself. The parents who raised you in the faith hear "I no longer believe what you taught me" as "I no longer value what you gave me." The translation is incorrect, but the pain is real.

## When Your Parents Think You Have Left God

The most common version of this conflict runs downhill, from parents to adult children. The parents hold a faith they received from their own parents and transmitted, at considerable cost and effort, to the next generation. They chose a church, enrolled their children in Sunday school, said grace before meals, prayed at bedtime, sacrificed vacations for mission trips, and organized their entire family life around a set of convictions they regarded as the most important thing they could pass on. And now their adult child has come home and announced, or more commonly, gradually revealed through a thousand small signals, that those convictions are no longer theirs.

The parental response is almost always a version of grief, though it rarely presents itself that way. It presents as anger: "How could you throw away everything we taught you?" It presents as guilt: "Where did we go wrong?" It presents as fear: "Are you going to hell?" It presents as desperate intervention: the book left on the pillow, the pastor's phone call, the tearful conversation that is really an ultimatum dressed in love.

What the parents rarely understand, because the experience is genuinely outside their frame of reference, is that their child has not abandoned the faith carelessly. The faith transition that brings an adult child into conflict with believing parents is almost never the result of laziness, rebellion, or moral failure. It is almost always the result of a long, agonizing process in which the child has wrestled with questions the parents never asked, encountered evidence the parents never considered, and arrived at conclusions the parents cannot process. The child has not thrown anything away. They have outgrown the container.

The theologian James Fowler's stages of faith development are useful here, though not as a weapon. Fowler identified six stages of faith, each more complex and differentiated than the last. Many adults never progress beyond Stage 3, what Fowler called "Synthetic-Conventional" faith, in which beliefs are held because they are shared by the community and have never been subjected to critical examination. The transition to Stage 4, "Individuative-Reflective" faith, in which beliefs are examined, questioned, and either claimed personally or released, is one of the most disruptive experiences in human development. It looks, from the outside, like destruction. From the inside, it is the terrifying and necessary process of building a faith that can bear the weight of an adult life.

## When Your Children Think You Are Brainwashed

The conflict also runs uphill. There are parents whose adult children have concluded, sometimes gently, sometimes with contempt, that their parents' faith is a delusion, a coping mechanism, or a symptom of insufficient education. The condescension is particularly painful because it reverses the authority structure of the family: the child who once looked up to you now looks down on you, and the thing they look down on is the thing you hold most sacred.

This is the less-discussed direction of the faith-family conflict, but it is no less common and no less painful. The secularized adult child who rolls their eyes at prayer, who makes dismissive comments about church, who sends articles debunking religion as if they are doing their parents a favor, this child is operating from a position of intellectual confidence that may or may not be justified, but that functions, in the family system, as a form of disrespect. The parent's faith is not a problem to be solved. It is a life that has been lived, a framework that has sustained them through grief, loss, failure, and the ordinary weight of existence. To treat it as a delusion is to dismiss the person who holds it.

The honest truth is that both directions of this conflict involve a failure of imagination, the inability to conceive that a person you love and respect could hold a position you find untenable. The parent cannot imagine how a thoughtful person could abandon the faith. The adult child cannot imagine how a thoughtful person could maintain it. Both are wrong. Thoughtful people, with access to the same evidence, reach different conclusions about the most fundamental questions of existence. This has been true for the entire history of human thought, and it will remain true long after your family argument is over.

## The Specific Pain of Shared Holidays

Holidays concentrate the conflict into a single day, a single table, a single prayer that someone at the table no longer believes in and someone else at the table considers the most important moment of the meal. Christmas, Easter, Thanksgiving, these are the dates on which the theological divide becomes physically present, sitting across from you, passing the potatoes.

The believing parent who insists on the traditional prayer before the Christmas meal is not merely saying grace. They are, in the experience of the adult child who has left the faith, asserting a reality the child can no longer affirm. The adult child who refuses to bow their head is not merely declining a ritual. They are, in the experience of the parent, rejecting the family's deepest identity. Both interpretations are real. Neither is complete. And the only way through is the willingness to hold both realities simultaneously, to let the prayer happen without demanding participation, and to let the non-participation happen without interpreting it as an attack.

Some families develop rituals that honor both realities. A moment of silence rather than a spoken prayer. A gratitude practice that does not require theological commitment. A new tradition that belongs to the whole family as it is now, not as it was. These accommodations are not compromises in the pejorative sense. They are creative acts of love, the family's effort to build a container large enough to hold all of its members, even the ones who have changed.

## Maintaining Relationship Across the Divide

The first principle of maintaining relationship across a theological divide is the simplest and the hardest: stop trying to fix each other. The parent who is constantly slipping devotional books into care packages is not expressing love. They are expressing the conviction that their child is broken and needs repair. The adult child who is constantly sending secular critiques of religion is not sharing interesting reading. They are expressing the conviction that their parent is deluded and needs correction. Both gestures, however well-intentioned, communicate the same message: "I cannot accept you as you are."

The second principle is to learn the difference between your grief and their problem. If your child has left the faith, your grief is legitimate. But it is your grief, not their crisis. Processing that grief is your responsibility, through prayer, through conversation with a trusted friend or counselor, through the slow work of releasing the outcomes you cannot control. It is not your child's responsibility to manage your grief by pretending to believe what they do not believe. The moment you make your emotional wellbeing contingent on their theological compliance, you have weaponized the relationship.

The third principle is to find the ground that remains. Even in families where the theological divide is total, there is almost always shared ground: shared values (honesty, compassion, justice), shared loves (family, nature, art, good food), shared history (the stories, traditions, and inside jokes that constitute the fabric of family life). A family that cannot worship together can still eat together, laugh together, serve together, and show up for each other in crisis. These shared practices are not a consolation prize for the loss of shared faith. They are the substance of family life, and they have their own integrity and their own capacity to bear the weight of love.

## Setting Boundaries Without Severing Ties

Boundaries are not walls. This distinction is crucial, because in families where faith is contested, both sides tend to confuse the two. The parent who cannot stop proselytizing needs a boundary, not a wall: "Mom, I love you. I know my faith journey worries you. But I need you to stop bringing it up every time we talk. If you keep doing it, I will have to limit our conversations, and I do not want to do that." The adult child who cannot stop mocking their parent's faith needs the same: "I am glad you have found a way of seeing the world that works for you. But when you dismiss what I believe, it hurts me. I need you to stop."

These conversations are excruciating. They require the willingness to name the harm without abandoning the relationship, to say, in effect, "What you are doing is hurting me, and I am asking you to stop, but I am not going anywhere." The boundary preserves the relationship by protecting it from the behavior that is destroying it. The wall terminates the relationship altogether. The goal is the boundary, not the wall.

There are situations in which the wall is necessary. When the family member's behavior crosses from disagreement into abuse, when the proselytizing becomes harassment, when the dismissal becomes contempt, when the theological difference is used as a weapon to control, shame, or manipulate, the wall is a legitimate act of self-preservation. But it should be the last resort, not the first response, and it should be accompanied by the honest acknowledgment that you are making a choice with consequences you cannot fully foresee.

The practical mechanics of boundaries in faith-divided families deserve specific attention. A boundary is most effective when it is stated clearly, maintained consistently, and accompanied by a visible demonstration of continued love. The family member who sets a boundary about religious conversations but then shows up faithfully for birthdays, calls regularly about non-theological matters, and demonstrates genuine interest in the other person's life is communicating something essential: "I am not rejecting you. I am protecting our relationship from the one thing that is destroying it." The boundary without the continued presence is experienced as rejection. The continued presence without the boundary is experienced as permission to continue the harmful behavior. Both elements are necessary.

Time is an underestimated factor in these conflicts. The acute crisis of discovery, the initial revelation that a family member's faith has changed, is almost always the worst moment. Emotions are raw, fears are at their peak, and neither side has developed the capacity to hold the new reality. Six months later, the situation is usually different. A year later, more different still. Families that can survive the initial shock often find, over time, that the theological divide does not determine the quality of the relationship nearly as much as they feared. The relationship adjusts. New patterns emerge. The family discovers that it is larger than its theology, that its bonds are deeper than its beliefs, and that love, while not omnipotent, is remarkably durable.

The deepest truth about faith transitions and family conflict is that they expose the quality of the family's love. A family that can only love each other when they agree about God does not actually have the kind of love that God demands. The love described in 1 Corinthians 13, love that is patient, kind, that does not insist on its own way, that bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things, is precisely the love that is needed when the agreement breaks down. It is easy to love someone who shares your faith. It is the work of a lifetime to love someone who does not. And it may be that this particular work is the one your faith was always preparing you for.
